claim: A leading theory holds that neurodevelopmental brain disorders arise from imbalances in excitatory and inhibitory (E/I) brain circuitry.
source: A leading theory holds that neurodevelopmental brain disorders arise from imbalances in excitatory and inhibitory (E/I) brain circuitry.
evidence: This is a statement about existing theory in the field, supported by the broader context of the manuscript and citations throughout.

claim: The E/I imbalance model cannot account for joint alterations in the observed neural firing rates and correlations.
source: (1) The E/I imbalance model cannot account for joint alterations in the observed neural firing rates and correlations
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by computational simulations and data analysis presented in the manuscript.

claim: Neural circuit function is vastly more sensitive to changes in some cellular components over others.
source: (2) Neural circuit function is vastly more sensitive to changes in some cellular components over others
evidence: This finding is stated in the abstract and demonstrated through parameter sensitivity analysis in Figure 3.

claim: The direction of circuit alterations in Fmr1 KO mice changes across development.
source: (3) The direction of circuit alterations in Fmr1 KO mice changes across development.
evidence: This finding is stated in the abstract and demonstrated through logistic model fitting to Ca2+ imaging data across developmental timepoints in Figure 5.

claim: The E/I imbalance model was first proposed as a model for autism.
source: First proposed as a model for autism (Rubenstein and Merzenich, 2003)
evidence: This is supported by citation to Rubenstein and Merzenich, 2003.

claim: The E/I imbalance concept has been applied to schizophrenia, Rett syndrome, fragile-X syndrome, tuberous sclerosis, and Angelman Syndrome.
source: the concept has since been applied to many other brain disorders, including Schizophrenia, Rett syndrome, fragile-X syndrome, tuberous sclerosis, and Angelman Syndrome.
evidence: This is a statement about the application of the E/I imbalance model to various disorders, supported by the broader literature.

claim: Several studies have found evidence that the E/I balance is upset in multiple brain disorders.
source: Although several studies have found evidence that the E/I balance is indeed upset in multiple brain disorders (Bateup et al., 2011; Dani et al., 2005; Gibson et al., 2008; Kehrer et al., 2008; Wallace et al., 2012)
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to published studies.

claim: Fragile-X Syndrome and autism have been associated with an excess of excitation.
source: Fragile-X Syndrome and autism have been associated with an excess of excitation (Gibson et al., 2008; Lee et al., 2017; Nelson and Valakh, 2015)
evidence: This claim is stated in the text and illustrated in Figure 1A, supported by citations.

claim: Rett Syndrome has been associated with an excess of inhibition.
source: while Rett Syndrome has been associated with an excess of inhibition (Dani et al., 2005).
evidence: This claim is stated in the text and illustrated in Figure 1A, supported by citation.

claim: No treatment for a neurodevelopmental disorder based on GABAergic-based interventions has yet been approved.
source: Although clinical trials for such GABAergic-based interventions are ongoing (Braat and Kooy, 2015), no treatment for a neurodevelopmental disorder based on this principle has yet been approved.
evidence: This is a factual statement about the status of clinical treatments, supported by citation to ongoing trials.

claim: The only change detected in mean firing rates was a decrease in firing probability in WT between P14–16 and P30–40 (p=0.027).
source: For mean firing rates, the only change we detected was a decrease in firing probability in WT between P14–16 and P30–40 (p=0.027)
evidence: This is a statistical finding from analysis of Ca2+ imaging data.

claim: WT mice showed an increased standard deviation of firing rates between P14–16 and P30–40 (p=0.015).
source: which was coupled with an increased s.d. of firing rates (p=0.015).
evidence: This is a statistical finding from analysis of Ca2+ imaging data.

claim: P9–11 KO animals had a higher firing rate standard deviation than WT (p=0.031).
source: We also detected a higher firing rate s.d. in P9–11 KO animals than WT (p=0.031).
evidence: This is a statistical finding from analysis of Ca2+ imaging data.

claim: There was a substantial decrease in pairwise correlations in both genotypes across development.
source: Finally, as previously reported (Golshani et al., 2009; Gonçalves et al., 2013; Rochefort et al., 2009), we found a substantial decrease in pairwise correlations in both genotypes across development
evidence: This finding is supported by data analysis and previous publications.

claim: KO animals had slightly higher correlations than WT at P9–11 (p=0.029).
source: with slightly higher correlations in KO animals than WT at P9–11 (p=0.029)
evidence: This is a statistical finding from analysis of Ca2+ imaging data.

claim: KO animals had slightly higher correlations than WT at P14–16 (p=0.047).
evidence: This is a statistical finding from analysis of Ca2+ imaging data.

claim: The L2/3 computational model consisted of 1700 excitatory pyramidal neurons, 115 5HT3AR-expressing neurons, 70 parvalbumin-expressing (PV) neurons, and 45 somatostatin-expressing (SOM) neurons.
source: The L2/3 computational model we built (Figure 2A, see Materials and methods for details) consisted of four interconnected populations of leaky integrate-and-fire neurons: one group of 1700 excitatory (E) pyramidal neurons and three groups of inhibitory neurons: 115 5HT3AR-expressing neurons, 70 parvalbumin-expressing (PV) neurons, and 45 somatostatin-expressing (SOM) neurons.
evidence: This describes the structure of the computational model built by the authors.

claim: The L2/3 circuit was driven by a separate population of 1500 L4 excitatory neurons.
source: This L2/3 circuit was driven by a separate population of 1500 L4 excitatory neurons.
evidence: This describes the input structure of the computational model.

claim: Cellular numbers, intrinsic properties, synaptic strengths, and connectivity statistics were taken from published in vitro data from P17–22 wild-type mice.
source: Cellular numbers, intrinsic properties, synaptic strengths, and connectivity statistics were taken from published in vitro data from P17–22 wild-type mice (Avermann et al., 2012; Lefort et al., 2009; Tomm et al., 2014).
evidence: This describes the source of parameters for the computational model, supported by citations.

claim: Twitching a whisker activates, on average, only ~20% of L2/3 neurons in its corresponding barrel.
source: For example, twitching a whisker activates, on average, only ~20% of L2/3 neurons in its corresponding barrel, each of which typically emits only one action potential (Clancy et al., 2015; Kerr et al., 2007; Sato et al., 2007).
evidence: This is a factual statement about neural responses supported by citations.

claim: L2/3 neurons typically emit only one action potential in response to whisker stimulation.
source: For example, twitching a whisker activates, on average, only ~20% of L2/3 neurons in its corresponding barrel, each of which typically emits only one action potential (Clancy et al., 2015; Kerr et al., 2007; Sato et al., 2007).
evidence: This is a factual statement about neural responses supported by citations.

claim: The mean response probability of each neuron in the simulation increased from zero to one monotonically with increasing L4 activity level.
source: We found that the mean response probability of each neuron in the simulation increased from zero to one monotonically with increasing L4 activity level.
evidence: This is a finding from the computational simulations shown in Figure 2.

claim: The sigmoidal-shaped response profile of simulated L2/3 neurons mimics the spiking response of mouse L2/3 pyramidal cells to extracellular L4 stimulation in vitro.
source: This sigmoidal-shaped response profile of simulated L2/3 neurons mimics the spiking response of mouse L2/3 pyramidal cells to extracellular L4 stimulation in vitro (Elstrott et al., 2014)
evidence: This claim compares simulation results to experimental data, supported by citation.

claim: The sparse, noisy and distributed network responses were reminiscent of in vivo activity following whisker stimulation.
source: while the sparse, noisy and distributed network responses were reminiscent of in vivo activity following whisker stimulation (Clancy et al., 2015; Kerr et al., 2007).
evidence: This claim compares simulation results to in vivo data, supported by citations.

claim: Each cell type falls into a distinct cluster in the two-dimensional slope-threshold space.
source: When we plotted the fitted slope and threshold values for each neuron against each other, we found that each cell type falls into a distinct cluster in this two-dimensional space.
evidence: This is a finding from analysis of simulation results shown in Figure 2D.

claim: All PV inhibitory neurons had a low slope and low threshold.
source: For example, all PV inhibitory neurons had a low slope and low threshold
evidence: This is a specific finding from the simulation results shown in Figure 2D.

claim: SOM inhibitory neurons had a steep slope and moderate threshold.
source: whereas SOM inhibitory neurons had a steep slope and moderate threshold.
evidence: This is a specific finding from the simulation results shown in Figure 2D.

claim: The biophysical circuit model contained 100 parameters.
source: The biophysical circuit model contained 100 parameters (Materials and methods).
evidence: This describes the complexity of the computational model.

claim: 76 of the model parameters were varied in turn by ±20% for sensitivity analysis.
source: To test this, we varied 76 of the model parameters in turn by ±20%, and repeated the entire set of simulations for each case (Materials and methods).
evidence: This describes the methodology for parameter sensitivity analysis.

claim: Increasing the amplitude of postsynaptic potentials of excitatory synapses from L4 to L2/3 excitatory neurons shifted the logistic threshold parameter of all cell types leftwards to lower values.
source: First, when we increased the amplitude of postsynaptic potentials (PSPs) of excitatory synapses from L4 to L2/3 excitatory neurons, we found that the logistic threshold parameter of all cell types shifted leftwards to lower values (Figure 3A left)
evidence: This is a finding from parameter sensitivity analysis shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Increasing the PSP amplitude of recurrent connections between L2/3 excitatory neurons resulted in excitatory and SOM inhibitory neurons having increased slope parameters relative to default, with little change in their threshold parameters.
source: In contrast, when we increased the PSP amplitude of a different excitatory synapse, the recurrent connections between L2/3 excitatory neurons, we found (Figure 3A center) that excitatory and SOM inhibitory neurons had increased slope parameters relative to default, with little change in their threshold parameters.
evidence: This is a finding from parameter sensitivity analysis shown in Figure 3A.

claim: When recurrent E-E connections were increased, 5HT3AR inhibitory neurons had decreased slopes and thresholds.
source: At the same time, 5HT3AR inhibitory neurons had decreased slopes and thresholds
evidence: This is a finding from parameter sensitivity analysis shown in Figure 3A.

claim: When recurrent E-E connections were increased, PV neurons had little change at all.
source: while PV neurons had little change at all.
evidence: This is a finding from parameter sensitivity analysis shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Increasing the probability of inhibitory synaptic connections from L2/3 PV interneurons to L2/3 excitatory neurons resulted in excitatory neurons having a marginally lower slope and increased threshold.
source: As a third example, we increased the probability of inhibitory synaptic connections from L2/3 PV interneurons to L2/3 excitatory neurons (Figure 3A right). In this case, we found that excitatory neurons had a marginally lower slope and increased threshold
evidence: This is a finding from parameter sensitivity analysis shown in Figure 3A.

claim: The magnitude of the shift in circuit response varied from parameter to parameter.
source: Overall, we found a very heterogeneous picture. First, the magnitude of the shift in circuit response varied from parameter to parameter (Figure 3B–C).
evidence: This is a summary finding from the comprehensive parameter sensitivity analysis shown in Figure 3.

claim: Varying some parameters had large effects while varying other parameters had little effect.
source: Varying some parameters, such as the first two examples given above, had large effects, whereas varying other parameters such as wI5htE (the strength of synapses from 5HT3AR inhibitory neurons to E neurons) or τmIsom (the membrane time constant of SOM inhibitory neurons) had little effect.
evidence: This is a finding from parameter sensitivity analysis.

claim: The direction of shift in 2-D slope-threshold space depended on which parameter was altered.
source: Second, the direction of shift in 2-D slope-threshold space also depended on parameter (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is a finding from parameter sensitivity analysis shown in Figure 3C.

claim: All four quadrants of the slope-threshold plane could be reached by various subsets of the model parameters.
source: All four quadrants of the slope-threshold plane could be reached by various subsets of the model parameters.
evidence: This is a finding from parameter sensitivity analysis shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Basic knowledge of whether a component was 'excitatory' or 'inhibitory' was insufficient to predict the direction of slope-threshold change.
source: Third, basic knowledge of whether a component was 'excitatory' or 'inhibitory' was insufficient to predict the direction of slope-threshold change.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the parameter sensitivity analysis.

claim: The two glutamatergic projections considered in Figure 3A had distinct effects on circuit function.
source: For example, the two glutamatergic projections considered in Figure 3A had distinct effects on circuit function.
evidence: This is a specific example illustrating the heterogeneity of parameter effects.

claim: The L2/3 somatosensory cortex circuit has extremely varied sensitivities to changes in its cellular components.
source: In summary, these simulations indicate that the L2/3 somatosensory cortex circuit has extremely varied sensitivities to changes in its cellular components
evidence: This is a summary conclusion from the parameter sensitivity analysis.

claim: The eventual circuit-level consequences cannot be predicted from knowledge of the class of the perturbed neurotransmitter alone.
source: and that the eventual circuit-level consequences cannot be predicted from knowledge of the class of the perturbed neurotransmitter alone.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the parameter sensitivity analysis.

claim: The E/I imbalance model cannot account for the heterogeneous parameter sensitivities observed in the simulations.
source: Since the E/I imbalance model groups all excitatory and inhibitory components as respective equals, it cannot account for these results.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn by comparing the E/I imbalance model predictions to simulation results.

claim: Neural firing rate was greatest when threshold was low and slope was high in the logistic model.
source: Neural firing rate was greatest when threshold was low and slope was high (top left of phase plot, Figure 4C left)
evidence: This is a finding from analysis of the logistic model shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Correlations were greatest when both threshold and slope were high in the logistic model.
source: whereas correlations were greatest when both threshold and slope were high (top right of phase plot, Figure 4C right).
evidence: This is a finding from analysis of the logistic model shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Any change in the circuit's input-output function slope or threshold will in general have distinct effects on firing rate versus correlations.
source: This implies that any change in the circuit's input-output function slope or threshold will in general have distinct effects on firing rate versus correlations
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the logistic model analysis.

claim: A one-dimensional E/I balance rule that exclusively sought to normalize neural firing rates would leave neural correlations free to achieve arbitrary values.
source: This shows that a one-dimensional E/I balance rule that exclusively sought to normalize neural firing rates would leave neural correlations free to achieve arbitrary values.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the analysis shown in Figure 4D.

claim: Previous studies have found evidence for an E/I imbalance in ASD.
source: Previous studies have found evidence for an E/I imbalance in ASD (Lee et al., 2017; Nelson and Valakh, 2015).
evidence: This is a statement about previous research supported by citations.

claim: Fragile-X syndrome is the leading inherited cause of ASD.
source: Fragile-X syndrome is the leading inherited cause of ASD
evidence: This is a factual statement about Fragile-X syndrome.

claim: Fragile-X syndrome carries alterations in excitability.
source: and also carries alterations in excitability (Contractor et al., 2015).
evidence: This is a statement about Fragile-X syndrome supported by citation.

claim: The output statistics of the fitted logistic models matched well those of the target Ca2+ imaging data.
source: The output statistics of the fitted models matched well those of the target data (Figure 5–figure supplement 1).
evidence: This describes the quality of model fits to data, shown in supplementary figure.

claim: In young animals (P9–11), most fitted parameter points were scattered at high values of both slope and threshold.
source: We found that in young animals, P9–11, most points were scattered at high values of both slope and threshold (Figure 5B left).
evidence: This is a finding from fitting the logistic model to Ca2+ imaging data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: With age, the parameter fits for both genotypes moved south-west toward the low slope and low threshold region of parameter space.
source: With age, the parameter fits for both genotypes moved south-west toward the low slope and low threshold region of parameter space (Figure 5B center and right).
evidence: This is a finding from fitting the logistic model to Ca2+ imaging data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: In young animals (P9–11 and P14–16), the KO group had both higher slope and higher threshold than WT.
source: In young animals, P9–11 and P14–16, the KO group had both higher slope and higher threshold than WT
evidence: This is a finding from fitting the logistic model to Ca2+ imaging data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: In adult animals (P30–40), the KO group had a lower slope and lower threshold than WT.
source: whereas in adult animals, P30–40, the KO group had a lower slope and lower threshold than WT.
evidence: This is a finding from fitting the logistic model to Ca2+ imaging data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: There is an opposite direction of circuit parameter change in young Fragile-X mice compared to adults.
source: These results demonstrate an opposite direction of circuit parameter change in young Fragile-X mice compared to adults
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the logistic model fitting results.

claim: The opposite direction of circuit parameter change was not uncovered by measures of neural firing rates and correlations alone.
source: which was not be uncovered by measures of neural firing rates and correlations (Figure 1C).
evidence: This highlights the added value of the logistic model analysis compared to simple statistics.

claim: In young animals (P9–11), changes in the logistic threshold had substantial effects on both firing rates and correlation.
source: In young animals, P9–11, changes in the logistic threshold (solid bars in Figure 6) had substantial effects on both firing rates and correlation.
evidence: This is a finding from sensitivity analysis shown in Figure 6.

claim: Threshold sensitivity decreased with age from P9–11 to P14–16 (p≤0.013 for firing rates, p<0.01 for correlations).
source: This sensitivity decreased with age (p≤0.013 for firing rates, p<0.01 for correlations from P9–11 to P14–16)
evidence: This is a statistical finding from sensitivity analysis.

claim: In adult animals (P30-40), changes in threshold had relatively little effect on neural activity statistics.
source: so that in adult animals, P30-40, changes in threshold had relatively little effect on neural activity statistics.
evidence: This is a finding from sensitivity analysis.

claim: The firing rate sensitivity to slope increased from P9–11 to P14–16 (p<1e-6).
source: There, the firing rate sensitivity increased from P9–11 to P14–16 (p<1e-6) (Figure 6C)
evidence: This is a statistical finding from sensitivity analysis shown in Figure 6C.

claim: Correlation sensitivity to slope stayed approximately constant across development (p≥0.18).
source: while correlation sensitivity stayed approximately constant (p≥0.18) (Figure 6D).
evidence: This is a statistical finding from sensitivity analysis shown in Figure 6D.

claim: The quantitative relationships between neural activity statistics and the parameters of the logistic model are not fixed across development.
source: These results show that the quantitative relationships between neural activity statistics and the parameters of the logistic model, and perhaps also the underlying circuit components, are not fixed across development.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the developmental sensitivity analysis.

claim: Entropy is a quantity from information theory that puts a hard upper bound on the amount of information that can be represented by any coding system.
source: Entropy is a quantity from information theory, measured in bits, that puts a hard upper bound on the amount of information that can be represented by any coding system (Cover and Thomas, 2006).
evidence: This is a definition from information theory supported by citation.

claim: Entropy is typically highest when firing rates are high and correlations are low.
source: It is typically highest when firing rates are high and correlations are low.
evidence: This is a general property of entropy in neural systems.

claim: In young animals P9–11, a small number of activity patterns accounts for a large fraction of the probability mass.
source: In young animals P9–11, a small number of activity patterns accounts for a large fraction of the probability mass (Figure 7A left).
evidence: This is a finding from entropy analysis shown in Figure 7A.

claim: In older animals P14–16 and P30–40 the cumulative distributions shift rightwards so that more patterns are typically observed.
source: In contrast, in older animals P14–16 and P30–40 the cumulative distributions shift rightwards so that more patterns are typically observed (Figure 7A center, right).
evidence: This is a finding from entropy analysis shown in Figure 7A.

claim: For all age groups and both genotypes, entropy/neuron progressively decreased with the number of neurons analyzed.
source: For all age groups, and for both WT and Fmr1 KO animals, entropy/neuron progressively decreased with the number of neurons analyzed (Figure 7B).
evidence: This is a finding from entropy analysis shown in Figure 7B.

claim: In WT animals at P9–11, entropy/neuron was 0.38 bits (95% c.i. [0.35:0.41]).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from entropy analysis.

claim: In WT animals, entropy/neuron increased at P14–16 (p<0.001) to 0.50 bits (95% c.i. [0.48:0.52]).
source: before increasing at P14–16 (p<0.001) to 0.50 bits (95% c.i. [0.48:0.52])
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from entropy analysis with statistical significance.

claim: In WT animals, entropy/neuron decreased at P30–40 (p=0.028) to 0.45 bits (95% c.i. [0.42:0.48]).
source: before decreasing again at P30–40 (p=0.028) to 0.45 bits (95% c.i. [0.42:0.48]).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from entropy analysis with statistical significance.

claim: In Fmr1 KO animals at P9–11, entropy/neuron was 0.34 bits (95% c.i. [0.30:0.39]), not different from WT (p=0.19).
source: There, although entropy/neuron also began low at 0.34 bits (95% c.i. [0.30:0.39]), not different from WT (p=0.19)
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from entropy analysis with statistical comparison.

claim: In Fmr1 KO animals, entropy/neuron increased at P14–16 (p<0.001) to 0.465 bits (95% c.i. [0.45:0.48]), lower than WT (p=0.048).
source: when it increased at P14–16 (p<0.001) to 0.465 bits (95% c.i. [0.45:0.48]) it remained lower than for WT (p=0.048).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from entropy analysis with statistical comparisons.

claim: In Fmr1 KO animals, entropy continued to increase at P30–40 (p=0.033) to 0.51 bits (95% c.i. [0.47:0.55]), higher than WT (p=0.034).
source: Finally, instead of decreasing as in the WT case, entropy continued to increase in P30–40 Fmr1 KO animals (p=0.033) to 0.51 bits (95% c.i. [0.47:0.55]), higher than WT (p=0.034).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from entropy analysis with statistical comparisons.

claim: Fmr1 KO mice showed a monotonically increasing entropy/neuron from P9–11 to P30–40.
source: In summary, unlike WT animals, Fmr1 KO mice showed a monotonically increasing entropy/neuron from P9–11 to P30–40.
evidence: This is a summary of the entropy trajectory in KO mice.

claim: The direction of change in entropy between P14–16 and P30–40 was opposite for WT and Fmr1 KO animals.
source: Furthermore, the direction of change in entropy between P14–16 and P30–40 was opposite for WT and Fmr1 KO animals, decreasing in the former and increasing in the latter.
evidence: This is a summary comparison of entropy trajectories between genotypes.

claim: Entropy values estimated directly from Ca2+ imaging data agreed well with entropy estimates for synthetic data sampled from the previously fit logistic models.
source: These entropy values estimated directly from Ca2+ imaging data agreed well with entropy estimates for synthetic data sampled from the previously fit logistic models (Figure 7–figure supplement 1).
evidence: This validates the consistency between different analysis approaches.

claim: The hyperexcitability prediction of the E/I imbalance model is consistent with many of the symptoms of Fragile-X syndrome.
source: In the case of Fragile-X syndrome, the hyperexcitability prediction of the E/I imbalance model is consistent with many of the symptoms of the disease (e.g. seizures, hyperarousal, hyperactivity, hypersensitivity to sensory stimuli)
evidence: This is a statement about the consistency between model predictions and clinical symptoms.

claim: The hyperexcitability prediction is consistent with known pathogenic defects implicated in Fmr1 KO mice including diminished GABA signaling, exaggerated intrinsic excitability, and increased neuronal firing rates.
source: and the known pathogenic defects implicated in Fmr1 KO mice (diminished GABA signaling, exaggerated intrinsic excitability, increased neuronal firing rates; reviewed by Contractor et al., 2015).
evidence: This is a statement about known defects in Fmr1 KO mice supported by citation to a review.

claim: The E/I imbalance model was too inflexible to account for the joint alterations in both neural firing rates and correlations observed in Fragile-X model mice.
source: Here, we tested the hypothesis that the E/I imbalance model can account for alterations in other neural activity statistics beyond the mean firing rates; however, our results demonstrated that it was inadequate. The model was too inflexible to account for the joint alterations in both neural firing rates and correlations observed in Fragile-X model mice.
evidence: This is a primary conclusion of the study based on the analyses performed.

claim: Future studies of brain disorders may need to consider higher-dimensional models of neural circuit dysfunction.
source: This suggests that future studies of brain disorders may need to consider higher-dimensional models of neural circuit dysfunction.
evidence: This is a recommendation based on the study's findings.

claim: Many of the physiological component changes discovered in animal models may be entirely benign at the circuit level.
source: Its existence has two important implications for studies of brain disorders: first, many of the physiological component changes discovered in animal models may be entirely benign at the circuit level.
evidence: This is an implication drawn from the redundancy property observed in the model.

claim: Any treatment designed to correct circuit function is free to push the system by arbitrary amounts along insensitive directions in parameter space without consequence.
source: Second, any treatment designed to correct circuit function is free to push the system by arbitrary amounts along insensitive directions in parameter space without consequence, as long as it makes the correct perturbations along the sensitive directions.
evidence: This is an implication for treatment design based on the redundancy property.

claim: The insensitive directions form a null space, which is a subspace of the parameter space.
source: The insensitive directions form a null space, which is a subspace of the parameter space.
evidence: This is a mathematical characterization of the redundancy property.

claim: The parameter sensitivity analysis was linear and local to a particular point in the high-dimensional model parameter space, corresponding to WT P17-22 mice.
source: An important caveat to our parameter sensitivity analysis is that it was linear and local to a particular point in the high-dimensional model parameter space, corresponding to WT P17-22 mice.
evidence: This is a methodological limitation acknowledged by the authors.

claim: The particular parameter sensitivities would likely be different in other parts of parameter space, especially near bifurcations.
source: Since the circuit dynamics are nonlinear, it is likely that the particular parameter sensitivities would be different in other parts of parameter space, especially near bifurcations where qualitatively different dynamics emerge (Hirsch et al., 2013).
evidence: This is a speculation about the generalizability of findings, supported by citation.

claim: The redundancy property is widely preserved in computational models of other biological systems.
source: However, as long as the redundancy property is widely preserved, as suggested by studies on computational models of other biological systems (Fisher et al., 2013; Gutenkunst et al., 2007; Machta et al., 2013; Panas et al., 2015), then our conclusions for brain disorders remain valid.
evidence: This is a statement about the generality of the redundancy property supported by citations.

claim: Previous studies found that neural correlations decrease during development.
source: Previous studies had found that neural correlations decrease during development (Golshani et al., 2009; Rochefort et al., 2009)
evidence: This is a statement about previous research supported by citations.

claim: Early postnatal Fmr1 KO mice had higher correlations and firing rates than WT mice.
source: and that early postnatal Fmr1 KO mice had higher correlations and firing rates than WT mice (Gonçalves et al., 2013; La Fata et al., 2014).
evidence: This is a statement about previous research supported by citations.

claim: Circuit hypersynchrony may be a general defect in autism disorders.
source: Circuit hypersynchrony may be a general defect in autism disorders, as it is also found in mouse models of Rett syndrome (Lu et al., 2016).
evidence: This is a speculation about autism disorders supported by citation to Rett syndrome findings.

claim: Qualitatively different interventions may be needed at different stages of development in Fragile-X to shift cortical circuit function towards typical wild-type operation.
source: Taken together, these findings imply that qualitatively different interventions may be needed at different stages of development in Fragile-X, and perhaps other neurodevelopmental disorders, to shift cortical circuit function towards typical wild-type operation.
evidence: This is an implication for treatment drawn from the developmental findings.

claim: Spontaneous, intrinsic activity is ubiquitously present in mammalian cerebral cortex.
source: Spontaneous, intrinsic activity is ubiquitously present in mammalian cerebral cortex.
evidence: This is a general statement about cortical activity.

claim: Spontaneous activity is highly structured at multiple spatiotemporal scales.
source: It is highly structured at multiple spatiotemporal scales (Mitra et al., 2015; Ringach, 2009)
evidence: This is a statement about spontaneous activity supported by citations.

claim: Spontaneous activity interacts strongly with the signals evoked by sensory stimulation.
source: and interacts strongly with the signals evoked by sensory stimulation (Ringach, 2009).
evidence: This is a statement about spontaneous activity supported by citation.

claim: The patterns of spontaneous activity in neural populations are representative of the ensemble of activity patterns used by the brain to represent sensory stimuli.
source: Cellular-resolution recordings in animals have shown that the patterns of spontaneous activity in neural populations are representative of the ensemble of activity patterns used by the brain to represent sensory stimuli (Berkes et al., 2011; Luczak et al., 2009; Miller et al., 2014).
evidence: This is a statement about spontaneous activity supported by citations.

claim: The entropy of spontaneous activity in WT mouse somatosensory cortex follows an inverted-U shaped trajectory across development.
source: Here, we found that the entropy of spontaneous activity in WT mouse somatosensory cortex follows an inverted-U shaped trajectory across development
evidence: This is a finding from the entropy analysis.

claim: The entropy trajectory is dramatically altered in the Fmr1 KO mouse model of Fragile-X.
source: and that this trajectory is dramatically altered in the Fmr1 KO mouse model of Fragile-X (Figure 7).
evidence: This is a finding from the entropy analysis shown in Figure 7.

claim: The switch in the direction of entropy change from WT to KO during development mirrors the reversing seen in logistic model parameter changes.
source: Notably, this switch in the direction of entropy change from WT to KO during development mirrors the reversing we saw in logistic model parameter changes in Figure 5C.
evidence: This connects findings from entropy analysis to logistic model analysis.

claim: The findings suggest a perturbed trajectory of cortical development during the critical period in Fmr1 KO mice.
source: Together, these findings suggest a perturbed trajectory of cortical development during the critical period in Fmr1 KO mice (Meredith et al., 2012).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the findings supported by citation.

claim: The results cannot distinguish whether the observed perturbation in L2/3 activity statistics reflects a developmental delay or a permanently altered developmental trajectory.
source: However, our results cannot distinguish whether the observed perturbation in L2/3 activity statistics reflects a developmental delay, or a permanently altered developmental trajectory.
evidence: This is an acknowledged limitation of the study.

claim: The entropy of neural circuit activity may be optimally tuned at intermediate levels as a trade-off between maximizing representational capacity at high entropy versus maintaining error correction and regularization at low entropy.
